SECTION 5. 
THE LIMITS OF OBJECTIVE 
INTER >RETATION 
Just as ob,ective and subjective theories have influenced the law of 
contract formation, 
they have 
also influenced the law of contract 
interpretation. There may be little disagreement over the proposition 
that, where the parties hav in fact attached different meanings to their 
language, an objective standard 
hould determine which meaning will 
prevail. But the objectivists argu 
that even where the parties have in 
fact attached the same meaning to their language, an objective standard 
should determine the meaning, which might be different from parties' 
shared meaning. Judge Learned Hand, for example, said: "It is quite true 
that we commonly speak of a contract as a question of intent, and for 
most purpose5 it is a convenient paraphrase, accurate enough, but, 
strictly speai rng, untrue. It makes not the least difference whether a 
promisor actually intends that meaning which the law will impose upon 
his words. The whole House of Bishops might satisfy us that he had 
intended something else, and it would make not a particle of difference 
in his obligation. That obligation the law attaches to his act of using 
certain words, provided, of course, the actor be under no disability." 
Eustis Mining Co. v. Beer, Sondheimer & Co., 239 F. 976, 984 (S.D.N.Y.
